I think there's a sort of life-cycle of social media sites. First, they are young, sparsely populated and lack significant content. They are weakly policed, and manage to attract both the best and the worst people. They often are overly insular, but they can still provide highly stimulating content. Because they are weakly policed, you can escape from society's boundaries and explore ideas that you can't explore elsewhere. Then they grow, diversify and mature. The content tends to improve in the early stages of this. The content is still weakly policed, so you can still explore society's boundaries, but there's a greater diversity of ideas and you can avoid more of the irritating people. The website is still primarily attracting highly curious, independence-loving individuals. As the websites become more popular, people who aren't within that category start to flock to it. They call for increased restrictions on content. It's no longer enough to simply ignore the jerks; you have to shut it down. The members who loved the site when it was wild and free run away. The websites becomes duller and staler over time and eventually becomes a shell of its former self.

I typically find that I enjoy websites that are in the early stages the most.
